questions.title: Diagnosing Memory Leaks in Java
questions.question: How do you identify and fix memory leaks in a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Memory leak: objects not reachable via live references but preventing GC**
- **Symptoms: growing heap over time, increasing Full GC frequency, eventual OOM**
- **Heap dump: snapshot of all objects — analyze with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM**
- **Common causes: static collections, listeners not removed, ThreadLocal not cleared**
- **jcmd / jmap: trigger heap dumps from running JVM**
- **Actuator /actuator/heapdump: Spring Boot endpoint for heap dumps**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A memory leak in Java is when objects can't be garbage collected because some live reference (intentionally or accidentally) still points to them. The symptoms are characteristic: heap usage grows steadily over time, GC frequency increases, Old Gen fills up progressively, and eventually you get an OutOfMemoryError after hours or days of running.

To diagnose, I first confirm it's a leak by looking at heap usage trend over time in monitoring (Grafana/Prometheus). If heap grows without bound after GC cycles, it's a leak. Then I take a heap dump — either via `jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump` or via Spring Boot Actuator's `/actuator/heapdump` endpoint. I analyze it in Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) which can automatically identify the 'leak suspects' — objects taking the most retained heap.

Common causes: static collections that grow without bound (a cache without size limit), event listeners added but never removed, ThreadLocal values not cleaned up, and inner class references holding onto outer class instances.
